faq.a: It covers the most common pathogens, is inexpensive, and has low resistance rates in most East African settings.
faq.q: Why is amoxicillin preferred as first‑line therapy?

faq.a: Post‑auricular erythema, tenderness, swelling, or protrusion of the ear, especially with persistent fever.
Mild cases may improve with analgesia alone, but guidelines recommend antibiotics for children under 2 years or severe disease.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with ear pain, fever 38.5 °C, and a bulging tympanic membrane – what is your next step? — Start oral amoxicillin, give analgesia, arrange review in 48 h.
How does otitis media differ from otitis externa on examination? — AOM shows bulging TM, otitis externa shows painful external canal with normal TM.
A child with HIV on ART develops AOM; which organism should you consider and how does it affect antibiotic choice? — Consider Pseudomonas; may need broader‑spectrum agent like cefuroxime.
What are the red‑flag signs that mandate referral to ENT? — Post‑auricular swelling, persistent high fever, neurological symptoms, or no improvement after 48 h of appropriate antibiotics.
Why is macrolide monotherapy discouraged in this setting? — High local resistance of Streptococcus pneumoniae reduces efficacy and promotes resistance.

Explain the AAP severity staging for AOM and its impact on management. — Mild (pain only) may be observed; moderate (pain + fever) needs antibiotics; severe (pain, fever, systemic signs) requires prompt antibiotics and close follow‑up.
A patient cannot tolerate oral medication; what is the alternative route and drug? — Use intramuscular benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone, chosen for coverage and once‑daily dosing.
What complication can cause permanent hearing loss if untreated, and how is it prevented? — Chronic suppurative otitis media; early effective antibiotics and ear‑drainage prevent progression.
ai.title: Acute Otitis Media
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a common middle‑ear infection in children, especially in low‑resource settings. Prompt recognition, appropriate antibiotics and monitoring prevent complications such as mastoiditis or hearing loss.

b: Higher risk with day‑care attendance, smoke exposure, and malnutrition
sections.p: AOM is inflammation of the middle ear cavity, usually following viral upper‑respiratory infection that blocks the eustachian tube, allowing bacterial overgrowth.

t.b: Is there middle‑ear effusion and inflammation? Red bulging tympanic membrane, loss of landmarks, and reduced mobility confirm AOM.
Assesses tympanic membrane mobility; absent movement supports effusion.

b: Common pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (non‑typeable), Moraxella catarrhalis
In HIV‑positive or malnourished children, consider Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus aureus
Complications: mastoiditis, tympanic membrane perforation, hearing loss
sections.p: Diagnosis requires acute onset, middle‑ear effusion, and signs of inflammation. Severity is staged by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) criteria: mild (pain only), moderate (pain + fever), severe (pain, fever + systemic signs).

t.b: Leukocytosis (>12 × 10⁹/L) suggests bacterial cause; normal count does not rule out AOM.

b: Give analgesia (paracetamol) for pain and fever
Educate caregivers on ear‑drop safety and follow‑up
If no improvement, consider second‑line (e.g., cefuroxime) or referral for drainage
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, antibiotics may be limited; first‑line oral amoxicillin is preferred unless contraindicated. Monitoring for treatment failure (persistent pain >48 h, fever >72 h) is essential.

t.b: Assess hearing loss after repeated episodes; normal result reassures, abnormal prompts ENT referral.

b: AOM: bulging, erythematous TM; otitis externa: painful external canal, no TM bulge
Mastoiditis: post‑auricular swelling, tenderness, fever, possible displacement of ear
Serous otitis media: dull TM, no pain, often after URI
sections.p: Exam questions often test differentiation of AOM from otitis externa, mastoiditis, and serous otitis media, as well as appropriate antibiotic choice and recognition of red‑flag complications.

b: Relying on tympanometry when pneumatic otoscopy is sufficient
Using macrolides first line despite high resistance in the region
Missing mastoiditis signs and delaying referral
sections.p: Students frequently over‑investigate with tympanometry or CT scans, or prescribe broad‑spectrum antibiotics unnecessarily.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe ear pain with swelling behind the ear (mastoiditis)
Persistent fever >39 °C for >72 h despite antibiotics
